title: The Justice Gap: The Unmet Civil Legal Needs of Low-income Americans (2022)
pub: Legal Services Corporation, prepared by Mary C. Slosar (Slosar Research) with NORC at the University of Chicago
author: Legal Services Corporation

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report provides strong empirical context for the cluster’s access-to-justice discussion by documenting extensive unmet legal need and limited legal-aid capacity. However, it does not assess legal AI, jagged capability, verification, selective deployment or work redesign, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: Seven out of every 10 (71%) of these problems will either not receive any legal help or not receive enough legal help to be fully resolved.

st.t: LSC funding: Preservation came with reduced resources
st.an: The source strengthens the cluster’s funding analysis with concrete intake evidence that existing resources enable LSC-funded organizations to help only 51% of eligible problems presented to them. It also materially qualifies the finding by limiting its scope to LSC’s network rather than the full national justice gap.
qs: presented to legal aid organizations funded by LSC; while LSC is the largest funder of civil legal aid in the country, there are also many other legal aid organizations serving low-income communities that operate outside of LSC’s network.

st.t: Justice gap: Fair resolution exceeds legal assistance
st.an: LSC supports the cluster’s broad account by documenting unmet civil legal needs tied to housing, livelihoods, health care and family, while identifying cost, limited legal awareness, low confidence and practical intake barriers—not price alone. Its operational measures remain primarily assistance- and capacity-based rather than direct measures of fair substantive resolution.
qs: Indeed, they did not think a lawyer could help with 44% of their problems and were not sure for another 30%.

kp.k: Civil justice access depends heavily on financial resources
kp.d: LSC frames the justice gap as unmet civil legal need involving housing, livelihoods, health care, family and safety. The report generally contrasts the absence of a civil right to counsel with criminal legal assistance, while acknowledging civil-right-to-counsel exceptions. It provides evidence about access to justice rather than claims about AI.
qs: The justice gap is the difference between the civil legal needs of low-income Americans and the resources available to meet those needs.
In contrast, one generally has no right to counsel in civil matters where people might risk losing their homes, livelihoods, health care, or children.

kp.k: Findings combine nationally representative survey and provider intake evidence
kp.d: NORC surveyed 2,003 adults from households at or below 125% of FPL and 3,305 above that level, using its probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel. Telephone and web interviews in English and Spanish ran October 15–December 4, 2021. Separately, all LSC-funded organizations tracked eligible assistance requests over four weeks starting October 4, 2021. These sources measure different populations and should not be conflated.
qs: The survey included a sample of n=2,003 adults from households at or below 125% of the federal poverty level (FPL) and a sample of n=3,305 adults from households above 125% of FPL.
NORC fielded the survey for seven weeks from October 15 to December 4, 2021.
For the 2021 Intake Census, each organization tracked the requests for assistance that it received over a four-week period starting October 4, 2021.

kp.k: Approximately fifty million Americans fall within low-income population
kp.d: Using principally the 2021 CPS ASEC, which reflects 2020 income and household information, the report identifies approximately 50 million people below 125% of the poverty threshold, including 15.2 million children and 7.6 million seniors. Census poverty thresholds differ from the HHS poverty guidelines used for FPL and legal-aid eligibility. The South contains 22.2 million low-income residents; rural residents have a higher low-income rate than suburban/urban residents, 19% versus 15%.
qs: About 50 million Americans have household incomes below 125% of the poverty threshold.

Note that poverty thresholds are different from the poverty guidelines published by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which are used to determine one’s percent of federal poverty level (FPL) and eligibility for LSC-funded legal assistance.

kp.k: Civil legal problems are widespread and frequently multiple
kp.d: The survey examined 81 distinct problems across 10 categories over the preceding 12 months. Among low-income households, 74% experienced at least one problem, 62% at least two, 39% at least five, and 20% at least ten. Consumer issues affected 50%, health care 39%, income maintenance 34%, housing 33%, family and safety 26%, and education 19%. These are household prevalence estimates, not counts of court cases.
qs: The survey explored a total of 81 distinct problems, which are grouped into 10 categories for the purposes of this report.
74% of low-income households experienced at least one civil legal problem in the past year.
One-half (50%) of low-income households experienced a problem related to consumer issues.

kp.k: Eviction and domestic violence accompany concentrated additional legal problems
kp.d: The report describes an association consistent with a vicious cycle, rather than establishing causation. Among households facing eviction-related issues, 81% experienced five or more additional problems and 58% ten or more; among domestic-violence households, the corresponding figures were 87% and 62%. Counts exclude the eviction or domestic-violence problems defining those groups. Housing problems affected 43% of renter households versus 23% of homeowner households.
qs: Households that experienced issues with eviction or domestic violence are disproportionately more likely to face multiple problems.
This pattern can feed a vicious cycle of civil legal problems that is difficult to interrupt without legal help.

kp.k: Legal problems substantially affect finances, health and relationships
kp.d: The report defines substantial impact as respondents reporting effects 'very much' or 'severely'. Overall, 38% of low-income Americans personally experienced a problem with substantial negative household impact; 35% reported substantial financial effects and 31% mental or emotional health effects. Among people personally experiencing problems, 55% reported substantial overall effects. Housing, family and safety, employment, and income maintenance were especially impactful.
qs: Civil legal problems had a substantial negative effect on 55% of those who personally experienced a problem in the past year.
Indeed, 35% report substantial impacts on their household’s financial situation, and 31% report the same for their or other household members’ mental and emotional health.

kp.k: People rarely seek help, even for substantial problems
kp.d: Low-income Americans sought legal help for 19% of personally experienced problems with some negative impact, rising to 25% for substantial problems versus 14% for less impactful ones. Help-seeking was higher for wills and estates (41%) and family and safety (33%), which the report characterizes as more obviously legal. The wills-and-estates estimate has a small base of 64 problems.
qs: Low-income Americans sought legal help for 19% of their collective civil legal problems in the past year.
People are more likely to seek legal help for problems that are more obviously “legal” like those involving legal documents and court proceedings.

kp.k: Demand for lawyers extends beyond courtroom representation
kp.d: Among 822 problems about which respondents talked to a lawyer, desired assistance included specific legal advice (59%), representation (39%), paperwork or forms (35%), negotiation (30%), handling communications (28%), and locating online resources (24%). These categories describe multiple forms of assistance rather than mutually exclusive service shares. Among substantial problems for which help was sought, 66% did not receive all the help respondents said they needed.
qs: The most common type of legal help sought was legal advice about specific situations (59% of the times they sought legal help).
Other common types of help sought include representation in court (39%) and help filling out legal forms and documents (35%).
low-income Americans did not receive all of the help they needed for 66% of these substantial problems.

kp.k: Survey justice gap reaches ninety-two percent for substantial problems
kp.d: The survey-based measure combines problems for which no legal help was sought with those for which help was sought but respondents reported insufficient assistance. It reaches 93% across personally experienced problems with any negative impact, 92% for substantial problems, and 94% for less impactful problems. These are problem-level measures, not percentages of individuals denied counsel or direct measures of unsuccessful legal outcomes.
qs: Low-income Americans did not receive any legal help or enough legal help for 92% of the problems that substantially impacted them in the past year.
Problems not receiving any legal help: The subset of problems for which they did not seek any legal help.

kp.k: Knowledge, confidence and cost constrain access to help
kp.d: Respondents did not believe lawyers could help with 44% of their problems and were unsure for another 30%. Only 28% believed people like them receive fair treatment in the civil legal system. Some 53% had low confidence or uncertainty about finding affordable counsel. Among people not seeking help for at least one problem, 46% cited cost; among those seeking but not obtaining all desired help, 61% cited expense, although that estimate has a small base of 110 respondents.
qs: low-income Americans did not know if a lawyer could help resolve 74% of their problems.
Only 28% of low-income Americans believe that people like them are treated fairly in the U.S. civil legal system.
Among those who did not seek legal help for at least one of their recent civil legal problems, nearly one-half (46%)49 cited concerns about cost as a reason why.

kp.k: Higher incomes improve access particularly for consequential problems
kp.d: Comparing households at or above 400% of FPL with those at or below 125%, substantial-problem help-seeking was 32% versus 25%, and the survey justice gap was 78% versus 92%. Confidence in finding affordable counsel was 73% versus 45%; belief in using the system to enforce rights was 59% versus 39%. Knowledge of lawyers' potential usefulness differed only slightly across income groups. For less impactful problems, unmet-help measures remained similar at 93%–94%.
qs: Regardless of income, most Americans either did not think that lawyers could help them with these sorts of problems (44% to 47%) or they were not sure about it (19% to 30%).
higher-income Americans are a full 28 percentage points more likely than low-income Americans to express this confidence (73% versus 45%).

kp.k: Pandemic-related problems exhibit wider income disparities in assistance
kp.d: The report finds that 33% of low-income Americans personally experienced a pandemic-related civil legal problem, compared with 18% of those at or above 400% of FPL. Attribution to the pandemic was respondent-reported, not a causal estimate. For substantial pandemic-related problems, the justice gap was 91% versus 68%, a 23-percentage-point disparity, compared with eight points for other substantial problems. The higher-income pandemic estimate rests on a small base of 103 problems.
qs: One-third (33%) of all low-income Americans personally experienced at least one civil legal problem related to the COVID-19 pandemic in the past year.
This translates to an income disparity of 23 percentage points (91% versus 68%).
Table 5C also makes clear that this income disparity is significantly greater for pandemic-related problems compared to other problems (23 versus 8 percentage points).

kp.k: Legal aid intake represents only part of total need
kp.d: Approximately 147,000 unique eligible problems recorded during the four-week intake census yield an annual projection of 1.9 million, assuming a typical intake period. This covers completed eligibility intake at LSC-funded organizations, not all legal aid or all unmet need. The analysis excludes conflicts-of-interest requests and allocates 17,730 pending cases proportionately across service categories. Eligibility generally uses 125% of FPL, with specified regulatory exceptions allowing service up to 200%.
qs: Assuming these four weeks represent intake activity for a typical four-week period in the year, this translates to an estimated 1.9 million eligible problems over the course of a year.
LSC’s 2021 Intake Census counts only problems that went through the full intake process to determine eligibility
There were 17,730 pending cases (out of a total of 146,724 eligible cases).

kp.k: Providers ration assistance across service intensity and legal need
kp.d: LSC-funded organizations provided some assistance for 51% of eligible problems. Among served problems, 28% received general information and self-help resources, 51% brief services and advice, and 21% extended services. Housing accounted for 36% and family and safety for 28% of served problems. The report links these priorities to substantial impacts and organizations' case-acceptance guidelines under resource constraints.
qs: The level of legal help an organization dedicates to a given problem depends on at least two factors: the type of help needed in order to resolve a problem and the resources available to meet that need.
Nearly two-thirds (64%) of all the problems receiving legal help from LSC-funded organizations are either related to housing (36%) or related to family and safety (28%).

kp.k: Resource shortages leave most eligible intake needs insufficiently served
kp.d: The intake-based justice gap is 71%, approximately 1.4 million eligible problems annually: 49% receive no help and 22% receive some but insufficient help. Among served problems, 56% were expected to receive enough help for resolution and 44% were not; these include organizational expectations, not exclusively observed completed outcomes. Of unserved problems, 52% fell outside priority guidelines, 18% within priorities lacked funds, and 30% involved contact or similar difficulties. LSC argues that better-resourced intake and follow-up could reduce the latter losses.
qs: Seven out of every 10 (71%) of these problems will either not receive any legal help or not receive enough legal help to be fully resolved.

This estimate is based on organizations’ reports of whether they have already provided enough help to fully resolve a problem or whether they expect to be able to do so given the resources they can devote to it.
The remaining 30% are turned away for reasons that are best described as ways that people can often “fall through the cracks.”

kp.k: Remote delivery imposed transition costs and digital access barriers
kp.d: The pandemic prompted legal aid organizations to acquire technology, train staff, revise communications and data protocols, and move outreach online. CARES Act funding largely covered technology upgrades, but staff time diverted from service delivery. Virtual courts required adaptation by lawyers and clients, with limited client internet access creating difficulties. Organizations closed fewer cases overall in 2020 than 2019, but more income-maintenance, employment and domestic-violence cases; the report qualifies the causal link to operational challenges.
qs: However, the transition to remote work used other resources (e.g., staff’s time) that would have otherwise been dedicated to providing legal services.
This was particularly challenging for clients, many of whom have limited access to the internet.
During the pandemic, many organizations recast parts of their outreach efforts into virtual events and social media activity.

kp.k: Design qualifications limit trend and subgroup interpretation
kp.d: LSC cautions against precise comparisons with its 2017 study because the designs differ and the 2022 report emphasizes substantial rather than any impact. Detailed help-seeking questions excluded problems with no overall negative impact and capped inquiry at ten problems per respondent, prioritizing certain categories when necessary. Units vary among individuals, households and problems; bases below 200 observations are flagged. The report's client stories illustrate assistance rather than providing representative effect estimates.
qs: Given differences in the design of the two studies, we caution against direct comparisons of precise estimates.
Bases with fewer than 200 observations are marked with an asterisk (*).
In the case that respondents experienced more than 10 problems that impacted their lives, the survey selected a subset of 10 of their problems about which to ask details.
